title: TP 01 · Introduction to time series
text:
This report answers Exercises 1–6 of Task 2 in I5TSA — TD/TP 1: Introduction, issued by Dr. Sim Tepmony and Mr. Nhim Malai. Tasks 1 (quiz) and 3 (take-home assignment) are outside the scope of this revision. The TSA package identifies its companion textbook as Cryer and Chan, Time Series Analysis with Applications in R, second edition.
The required plots are followed by evidence-based interpretations. Additional summaries, normal quantile–quantile (Q–Q) plots, and autocorrelation functions (ACFs) are exploratory supplements, not additional handout questions. The textbook exhibits themselves were not supplied: the plots below reproduce the requested series and plotting conventions without claiming an exact graphical facsimile.
Three distinctions guide the analysis:

Time dependence concerns how observations relate across time. Joining points preserves their order but does not imply that intervening values were observed.
Marginal distribution describes values at an individual time: for example, Gaussian, chi-square, or Student’s \(t\). Nonnormality does not imply dependence.
Sample appearance varies between realizations. Short runs, clusters, and extreme observations can occur in an independent process.

2 Reproducible setup and data audit
The analysis uses base R, TSA for datasets, and knitr for tables. Install project dependencies once with Rscript scripts/setup.R; package installation is deliberately excluded from the report. Render from the project root with quarto render TP01/tp01.qmd. Each simulation has a recorded seed, and the random-number generator is specified explicitly. Session and package versions are reported at the end.


Code
required <- c("TSA", "knitr")
missing <- required[!vapply(required, requireNamespace, logical(1),
                            quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing)) {
  stop("Install the required packages first: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "))
}

# Load datasets without attaching TSA, which also defines statistical functions.
data("larain", package = "TSA")
data("color", package = "TSA")
data("tempdub", package = "TSA")
RNGkind(kind = "Mersenne-Twister", normal.kind = "Inversion",
        sample.kind = "Rejection")
options(digits = 4)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%")

ink <- "#176B87"
accent <- "#A64B00"
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
lag1 <- function(x) {
  as.numeric(stats::acf(as.numeric(x), lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2])
}

series <- list(larain = larain, color = color, tempdub = tempdub)
stopifnot(
  all(vapply(series, is.ts, logical(1))),
  all(vapply(series, function(x) all(is.finite(x)), logical(1))),
  length(larain) == 115L, frequency(larain) == 1,
  all(start(larain) == c(1878, 1)), all(end(larain) == c(1992, 1)),
  length(color) == 35L, frequency(color) == 1,
  all(start(color) == c(1, 1)), all(end(color) == c(35, 1)),
  length(tempdub) == 144L, frequency(tempdub) == 12,
  all(start(tempdub) == c(1964, 1)), all(end(tempdub) == c(1975, 12))

3 Exercise 1 · Annual rainfall in Los Angeles
Question. Plot larain as a time series, corresponding to Exhibit 1.2.


Code
rain_year <- as.numeric(time(larain))
rain_min <- which.min(larain)
rain_max <- which.max(larain)
plot(larain, type = "o", pch = 16, cex = 0.45, col = ink,
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Annual rainfall (inches)",
     ylim = c(0, max(larain) * 1.14),
     main = "Annual rainfall in Los Angeles")
abline(h = mean(larain), col = accent, lty = 2)
text(rain_year[rain_max], larain[rain_max],
     labels = paste(rain_year[rain_max], fmt(larain[rain_max]), "in"),
     pos = 3, cex = 0.8)
text(rain_year[rain_min], larain[rain_min],
     labels = paste(rain_year[rain_min], fmt(larain[rain_min]), "in"),
     pos = 1, cex = 0.8)
legend("topright", "Sample mean", col = accent, lty = 2, bty = "n")








Figure 1: Annual Los Angeles precipitation, 1878–1992. The dashed line is the sample mean, not a fitted trend.







Code
observed_summary <- function(x) {
  c(N = length(x), Mean = mean(x), Median = median(x), SD = sd(x),
    Minimum = min(x), Maximum = max(x), `Lag-1 ACF` = lag1(x))
}

Interpretation. Rainfall fluctuates substantially: the observed minimum is 4.08 inches in 1953, and the maximum is 40.29 inches in 1884. The mean (14.89 inches) exceeds the median (14.14 inches), consistent with the influence of unusually wet years. These are extremes relative to this sample; the plot does not establish measurement errors or justify deleting them.
There is no clear sustained monotonic trend in this plot. Because observations are annual totals, within-year seasonality cannot be assessed. The lag-1 sample ACF is -0.033, indicating little observed linear association between adjacent years. A single coefficient, or an absence of obvious visual pattern, does not establish independence, stationarity, or the absence of longer-term climatic variation.

Interpretation. Measurements range from 63 to 87 with mean 74.89. Early batches are generally low, batches 11–18 are mostly higher, batches 19–23 return to lower values, and another high group appears around batches 25–28. These broad movements suggest persistence rather than purely isolated fluctuations. The lag-1 sample ACF is 0.528, appreciably larger than that of rainfall.
Only 35 batches are observed. They do not justify a claim of regular seasonality, a specific cycle length, or an identified change point. The plot motivates investigation of serial dependence and possible process changes without establishing their cause. No engineering tolerance limits are supplied, so these fluctuations cannot be classified as acceptable or unacceptable product quality.

4.1 Supplement · ACFs of the observed series
For lag \(k\), the sample ACF used here is
\[
\widehat\rho(k)=
\frac{\sum_{t=k+1}^{n}(x_t-\bar x)(x_{t-k}-\bar x)}
     {\sum_{t=1}^{n}(x_t-\bar x)^2}.
\]
It describes linear association, not every form of dependence. The dashed limits in Figure 3 are approximate pointwise white-noise reference limits, about \(\pm1.96/\sqrt{n}\). They are not simultaneous limits across all lags and do not constitute a test of independence. Interpretation also presumes a reasonably stable mean and variance; a changing mean can itself produce a large ACF. See the R ACF documentation.


Code
local({
  old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
  on.exit(par(old))
  stats::acf(as.numeric(larain), lag.max = 20,
             main = "Rainfall", xlab = "Lag (years)", col = ink)
  stats::acf(as.numeric(color), lag.max = 10,
             main = "Color", xlab = "Lag (batches)", col = ink)
})








Figure 3: Exploratory ACFs of rainfall and color. Lag units are years and batches, respectively; lag zero is one by definition.

title: TP 01 · Introduction to time series
text:
5 Framework for Exercises 3–5
A completely random process here means independent and identically distributed (iid) observations:
\[
X_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} F,\qquad t=1,\ldots,48.
\]
With finite variance, \(E(X_t)=\mu\), \(\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=\sigma^2\), and \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_t,X_{t-k})=0\) for nonzero \(k\). An iid process is strictly stationary and, with finite variance, weakly stationary. These are properties of the generating model, not conclusions established by inspecting 48 values.
Under the zero-mean convention, weak white noise has zero mean, constant finite variance, and zero autocovariance at nonzero lags. Independence is stronger than being uncorrelated. The normal and \(t_5\) simulations have zero mean; the raw chi-square simulation has mean 2, and its centered version \(X_t-2\) is white noise under this convention.

We generate three realizations of length 48 per distribution. Each seed is set once before replicate(), allowing the generator state to advance between realizations. Resetting the same seed inside each repetition would reproduce the same path. All generated paths are retained without selecting those that look most persuasive.
The helper displays each realization separately, using common vertical limits within each distribution. A paired normal Q–Q plot examines marginal shape: approximately straight points are compatible with a normal location-scale family, while systematic curvature suggests departures. It cannot diagnose temporal independence. Its line passes through sample quartiles and is not a confidence band.


Code
n <- 48L
B <- 3L

plot_runs <- function(runs, distribution, theoretical_mean) {
  old <- par(mfrow = c(ncol(runs), 2), mar = c(3.6, 4, 2.5, 1),
             mgp = c(2.2, 0.7, 0))
  on.exit(par(old))
  limits <- range(runs, theoretical_mean)
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(runs))) {
    x <- runs[, j]
    plot(seq_along(x), x, type = "o", pch = 16, cex = 0.5,
         col = ink, ylim = limits, xlab = "Time index", ylab = "Value",
         main = paste(distribution, "- realization", j))
    abline(h = theoretical_mean, col = accent, lty = 2)
    stats::qqnorm(x, pch = 16, cex = 0.55, col = ink,
                  ylim = limits, main = paste("Normal Q-Q - realization", j),
                  xlab = "Theoretical normal quantile", ylab = "Sample quantile")
    stats::qqline(x, col = accent, lty = 2)
  }
}

run_summary <- function(runs) {
  data.frame(
    Realization = seq_len(ncol(runs)), N = nrow(runs),
    Mean = colMeans(runs), Variance = apply(runs, 2, var),
    Minimum = apply(runs, 2, min), Maximum = apply(runs, 2, max),
    `Lag-1 ACF` = apply(runs, 2, lag1), check.names = FALSE
  )
}

6 Exercise 3 · Independent normal observations
Question. Generate 48 independent normal values, plot them, and repeat. Does the series look random?
We choose \(X_t\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,1)\), making the unspecified normal parameters explicit. Thus \(E(X_t)=0\), \(\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=1\), and \(\rho(k)=0\) for \(k\ne0\).

set.seed(2025)
normal_runs <- replicate(B, stats::rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1))
plot_runs(normal_runs, "N(0, 1)", theoretical_mean = 0)

Answer. The realizations fluctuate irregularly around zero, and apparent runs or local rises and falls differ between realizations. This appearance is compatible with randomness, but independence is specified by the simulation model, not established by the visual impression. A random process need not alternate signs regularly or have sample mean exactly zero.
Across these realizations, sample means range from -0.338 to 0.128, and sample variances range from 0.892 to 1.034. Such differences reflect sampling variation. The standard deviation of a sample mean is \(1/\sqrt{48}\approx0.144\), so moderate deviations from zero are expected. Q–Q departures at the extremes of a small sample do not, by themselves, establish that the specified normal generator is incorrect.

7 Exercise 4 · Independent chi-square observations
Question. Repeat with 48 independent chi-square values with two degrees of freedom. Does it look random and nonnormal?
For \(X_t\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\chi^2_2\),
\[
E(X_t)=2,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X_t)=4,\qquad
f(x)=\tfrac12 e^{-x/2}\quad(x>0).
\]
This is an exponential distribution with mean 2 and skewness 2. The R chi-square documentation gives the generator and distribution formulas.


Code
set.seed(2026)
chisq_runs <- replicate(B, stats::rchisq(n, df = 2))
plot_runs(chisq_runs, "Chi-square(2)", theoretical_mean = 2)








Figure 5: Three iid chi-square(2) realizations and normal Q–Q plots. Horizontal dashed lines mark the mean of 2; the raw series has not been centered.

Answer. The timing of high and low observations is irregular, as expected for iid draws. Nonnegative values and occasional large positive spikes reveal asymmetry more readily than in the normal experiment. The maximum over the three retained paths is 11.09; this is a simulation result, not an upper bound on the distribution. Curvature in the normal Q–Q plots helps distinguish this skewed marginal distribution from a Gaussian one.
These paths can look random and nonnormal because the properties concern different aspects of the process. Spikes do not imply serial dependence or data errors. The raw process has a positive mean; \(\varepsilon_t=X_t-2\) is zero-mean iid noise with variance 4. Subtracting 2 changes its location but neither its independence nor its skewness. The standard deviation of the sample mean is \(2/\sqrt{48}\approx0.289\), twice that of the standard-normal experiment.

title: TP 01 · Introduction to time series
text:
8 Exercise 5 · Independent Student’s t observations
Question. Repeat with 48 independent \(t\) values with five degrees of freedom. Does it look random and nonnormal?
For \(X_t\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}t_5\),
\[
E(X_t)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X_t)=\frac{5}{5-2}=\frac53.
\]
The distribution is symmetric with heavier tails than a normal distribution. Its excess kurtosis is \(6/(5-4)=6\), compared with zero for a Gaussian distribution. See the R Student’s t documentation for the generator, density, and mean/variance conditions.


Code
set.seed(2027)
t_runs <- replicate(B, stats::rt(n, df = 5))
plot_runs(t_runs, "Student t(5)", theoretical_mean = 0)








Figure 6: Three iid t(5) realizations and normal Q–Q plots. Horizontal dashed lines mark the theoretical mean of zero.

Answer. As in the normal experiment, paths fluctuate irregularly around zero. The largest observed absolute value across these paths is 9.05. The heavy-tailed model makes large excursions more likely but does not guarantee an obvious extreme in every 48 observations. A short \(t_5\) path may therefore resemble a normal path; nonnormality is less visually apparent than for \(\chi^2_2\).
When sufficiently extreme observations occur, a normal Q–Q plot tends to depart outward in the tails. At this sample size the pattern can be weak or uneven. We know the simulated population is nonnormal from its generating model, not from whether a particular realization passes a visual or formal normality check.
A fair comparison of tails. The raw \(t_5\) distribution also has greater variance than \(N(0,1)\), so larger raw excursions alone do not isolate tail shape. Set \(Z_t=\sqrt{3/5}\,X_t\) to give the \(t\) variable unit variance. Compare the probability of exceeding three population standard deviations in absolute value:

8.1 Supplement · Serial correlation in simulated paths


Code
local({
  old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
  on.exit(par(old))
  examples <- list("N(0, 1)" = normal_runs[, 1],
                   "Chi-square(2)" = chisq_runs[, 1],
                   "Student t(5)" = t_runs[, 1])
  for (nm in names(examples)) {
    stats::acf(examples[[nm]], lag.max = 10, ylim = c(-1, 1),
               main = nm, xlab = "Lag (observations)", col = ink)
  }
})








Figure 7: ACFs of the first realization from each model, selected in advance rather than for its appearance. Limits are approximate pointwise white-noise references.





The population ACF is zero at every positive lag for all three models, but the sample ACF need not be zero. R centers observations when estimating this ACF, including the raw chi-square values. With only 48 observations, the reference limits are approximately $$0.283; isolated crossings can occur by chance, especially when many lags or realizations are inspected. These limits are asymptotic and warrant caution for short, skewed, or heavy-tailed samples. No search for a favorable seed or repeated significance testing is used to certify independence.

9 Exercise 6 · Monthly temperatures in Dubuque
Question. Plot tempdub with monthly plotting symbols, following the convention in Exhibit 1.9.


Code
month_id <- as.integer(cycle(tempdub))
month_symbol <- substr(month.abb, 1, 1)
local({
  old <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
  on.exit({ layout(1); par(old) })
  layout(matrix(1:2, ncol = 1), heights = c(1, 0.16))
  par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
  plot(tempdub, type = "l", col = "grey75", xaxt = "n",
       xlab = "Year", ylab = expression("Monthly average temperature (" * degree * "F)"),
       main = "Monthly temperatures in Dubuque")
  axis(1, at = 1964:1976)
  points(time(tempdub), as.numeric(tempdub),
         pch = month_symbol[month_id], col = ink, cex = 0.75)
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot.new()
  legend("center", legend = month.abb, pch = month_symbol, col = ink,
         ncol = 6, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
})
month_mean <- tapply(as.numeric(tempdub), month_id, mean)
month_sd <- tapply(as.numeric(tempdub), month_id, sd)
coldest <- which.min(month_mean)
warmest <- which.max(month_mean)








Figure 8: Monthly average Dubuque temperatures, January 1964–December 1975, in degrees Fahrenheit. Letters identify months; repeated initials are resolved by calendar position and the legend.





Interpretation. The dominant feature is a strong annual seasonal cycle, with period 12 observations. Temperatures tend to peak in the middle of each calendar year and reach troughs near its beginning and end. Monthly symbols preserve calendar identity, making it easier to compare one January with another rather than with the preceding December alone.
Across the 12 years, the coldest month on average is January (16.61 °F) and the warmest is July (71.72 °F). Their mean difference is 55.11 °F. These are differences between monthly averages across years, not the observed range within every individual year.

title: TP 01 · Introduction to time series
text:
10 Conclusions
The observed series illustrate annual rainfall variation, persistence in industrial color measurements, and strong annual seasonality in monthly temperatures. The simulations show that independent observations can have Gaussian, skewed, or heavy-tailed distributions. Known population properties must be distinguished from chance features in short realizations. Time plots address temporal structure; Q–Q plots address marginal shape; neither alone proves independence or stationarity.

title: Empirical Autoregressive Modeling of Financial Asset Returns
text:
In quantitative finance and empirical asset pricing, modeling financial returns is foundational to risk management, algorithmic execution, and derivatives pricing. This case study applies the Box–Jenkins modeling strategy to daily closing prices from the benchmark EuStockMarkets dataset in R (1991–1998, \(N = 1,860\) daily observations per index), focusing on the FTSE 100 index.
We demonstrate the transition from non-stationary asset price levels (\(I(1)\)) to stationary continuously compounded log returns (\(I(0)\)). We rigorously evaluate the Weak-Form Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) and show that while daily index returns display statistically detectable first-order autoregressive persistence (\(\text{AR}(1)\) with \(\hat{\phi}_1 = 0.0678, p = 0.0066\)) due to market microstructure and non-synchronous trading, the economic magnitude is modest. Furthermore, residual diagnostics demonstrate the textbook stylized facts of financial time series: absence of linear serial correlation alongside pronounced volatility clustering and leptokurtosis, directly motivating the transition to ARCH/GARCH models.

title: Empirical Autoregressive Modeling of Financial Asset Returns
text:
1 Financial Econometric Foundations

1.1 The Random Walk and Martingale Difference Hypotheses
Let \(P_t\) denote the closing price of an asset at trading day \(t\). Under the classical Random Walk Hypothesis (Fama, 1970), price increments are independent and identically distributed:
\[
\ln(P_t) = \mu + \ln(P_{t-1}) + e_t, \qquad e_t \stackrel{i.i.d.}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2).
\]
A more general, economically grounded formulation is the Martingale Difference Hypothesis (MDH), which states that the conditional expectation of future price innovations given all publicly available market information \(\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\) is zero:
\[
E\bigl[P_t - P_{t-1} \mid \mathcal{F}_{t-1}\bigr] = 0 \iff E\bigl[r_t \mid \mathcal{F}_{t-1}\bigr] = \mu,
\]
where \(r_t = 100 \times \ln(P_t / P_{t-1})\) represents the percentage log return.


1.2 Why Index Returns Exhibit Weak Autocorrelation: Non-Synchronous Trading
If individual asset returns are martingales, why do composite market indices (such as the FTSE 100 or S&P 500) frequently display positive first-order autocorrelation (\(\phi_1 > 0\))?
As established by Lo and MacKinlay (1990) and Campbell, Lo, and MacKinlay (1997), broad market indices suffer from non-synchronous trading (or stale pricing): 1. Heavily traded, large-capitalization stocks incorporate market-wide macroeconomic shocks almost instantly at the end of the trading day. 2. Smaller, less liquid constituents of the index trade less frequently, and their recorded closing prices reflect earlier daytime information. 3. Consequently, information that moved large-cap stocks today only gets reflected in small-cap closing prices tomorrow, inducing a spurious positive lag-1 autocorrelation in the aggregate index:
\[
r_t^{\text{index}} = \mu + \phi_1 r_{t-1}^{\text{index}} + e_t, \qquad \phi_1 > 0.
\]

section: 2 Step 1: Data Preparation and Financial Returns Construction
text:
2 Step 1: Data Preparation and Financial Returns Construction

2.1 Purpose
To inspect the multidimensional structure of the EuStockMarkets dataset, compute continuously compounded log returns, and partition the data into in-sample estimation and out-of-sample forecast evaluation windows.


2.2 Statistical Concept
Financial asset prices \(P_t\) are strictly positive and typically non-stationary. Econometric analysis is performed on continuously compounded log returns:
\[
r_t = 100 \times \ln\left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}}\right) = 100 \times \bigl[\ln(P_t) - \ln(P_{t-1})\bigr],
\]
which possess convenient mathematical properties: 1. Time Additivity: Multi-period log return over \(k\) days equals the sum of single-day returns: \(r_{t, k} = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} r_{t-i}\). 2. Stationarity: Log-differencing eliminates stochastic trends, yielding a mean-reverting series.


2.3 R Implementation


Code
data(EuStockMarkets)

# Structural inspection
indices <- colnames(EuStockMarkets)
n_obs   <- nrow(EuStockMarkets)
freq_val <- frequency(EuStockMarkets) # 260 trading days per business year

# Select FTSE 100 index
ftse_price <- EuStockMarkets[, "FTSE"]

# Construct percentage log returns
r_ftse <- diff(log(ftse_price)) * 100
n_returns <- length(r_ftse)

# Check integrity
has_na   <- any(is.na(r_ftse))
has_dups <- any(duplicated(time(r_ftse)))

# In-sample / Out-of-sample Partition
# Train: first 1600 trading days (1991 to mid-1997)
# Test:  final 259 trading days (mid-1997 to 1998, exactly one business year)
train <- window(r_ftse, end = time(r_ftse)[1600])
test  <- window(r_ftse, start = time(r_ftse)[1601])

# Descriptive statistics function
calc_descriptives <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  m <- mean(x)
  s <- sd(x)
  skew <- sum((x - m)^3) / (n * s^3)
  kurt <- sum((x - m)^4) / (n * s^4) - 3 # Excess kurtosis
  c(
    N        = n,
    Mean     = m,
    SD       = s,
    Median   = median(x),
    IQR      = IQR(x),
    Min      = min(x),
    Max      = max(x),
    Skewness = skew,
    Kurtosis = kurt
  )
}

desc_table <- rbind(
  `Price Level (FTSE)` = calc_descriptives(as.vector(ftse_price)),
  `Daily Returns (Full)` = calc_descriptives(as.vector(r_ftse)),
  `Train Returns (1600)` = calc_descriptives(as.vector(train)),
  `Test Returns (259)`   = calc_descriptives(as.vector(test))
)

3 Step 2: Exploratory Data Analysis & Financial Time Series Dynamics

3.1 Purpose
To visually compare non-stationary price dynamics with mean-reverting daily returns and identify volatility clustering.


3.2 Statistical Concept
A stationary process fluctuates around a constant mean with constant variance. While daily returns fluctuate around an unconditional mean near zero, the magnitude of the fluctuations changes over time—a phenomenon known as Mandelbrot’s volatility clustering (1963): large returns (of either sign) cluster together in high-volatility regimes.


3.3 R Implementation


Code
par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(2.5, 4, 2, 1), oma = c(1, 0, 0, 0))

# 1. Price level
plot(ftse_price, col = "gray25", lwd = 1.3,
     ylab = "Index Level", xlab = "", main = "FTSE 100 Daily Closing Price (1991–1998)")
grid(col = "gray85")

# 2. Daily Log Returns
plot(r_ftse, col = "steelblue", lwd = 0.9,
     ylab = "Return (%)", xlab = "", main = "Daily Percentage Log Returns: r[t] = 100 * diff(log(P[t]))")
abline(h = mean(train), col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
abline(v = time(r_ftse)[1600], col = "darkorange", lty = 3, lwd = 1.5)
grid(col = "gray85")

# 3. Absolute Returns (Volatility Proxy)
plot(abs(r_ftse), col = "darkorange3", lwd = 0.9,
     ylab = "|Return| (%)", xlab = "Year", main = "Absolute Daily Returns |r[t]| (Instantaneous Volatility Proxy)")
abline(v = time(r_ftse)[1600], col = "darkorange", lty = 3, lwd = 1.5)
grid(col = "gray85")





Top panel: Daily FTSE 100 closing price level exhibiting strong non-stationary upward trend. Middle panel: Daily percentage log returns displaying mean reversion with volatility clustering. Bottom panel: Absolute daily returns |r_t| serving as an empirical proxy for conditional market volatility.






3.4 Output Interpretation

Price Trajectory: The FTSE 100 price level displays strong persistence and an upward secular trend without fixed mean, indicative of an \(I(1)\) integrated process.
Returns Trajectory: Returns rapidly oscillate around a horizontal center line (\(\mu \approx 0.05\%\)). There is no deterministic trend, confirming mean reversion.
Volatility Dynamics: Periods of quiet trading (e.g., 1993–1995) alternate with turbulent regimes characterized by large spikes in absolute returns (e.g., late 1992 and the 1997–1998 Asian/Russian financial crises).

section: 4 Step 3: Unit Root and Stationarity Testing
text:
4 Step 3: Unit Root and Stationarity Testing

4.1 Purpose
To verify through formal econometric testing that index prices are non-stationary (\(I(1)\)) and returns are stationary (\(I(0)\)).


4.2 Statistical Concept
The Augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) regression tests for the existence of a unit root:
\[
\Delta y_t = c + \beta t + \gamma y_{t-1} + \sum_{i=1}^k \psi_i \Delta y_{t-i} + e_t,
\]
under \(H_0: \gamma = 0\) (unit root) versus \(H_1: \gamma < 0\) (stationary).


4.3 R Implementation


Code
# ADF on Price level (with trend)
adf_price <- adf.test(ftse_price, alternative = "stationary")

# ADF on In-sample Returns
adf_return <- adf.test(train, alternative = "stationary")

adf_table <- data.frame(
  Series = c("FTSE 100 Price Level (P_t)", "FTSE 100 Log Returns (r_t)"),
  Test = "Augmented Dickey-Fuller",
  Lag_Order = c(adf_price$parameter, adf_return$parameter),
  Test_Statistic = c(round(adf_price$statistic, 4), round(adf_return$statistic, 4)),
  P_Value = c(round(adf_price$p.value, 4), adf_return$p.value),
  Decision = c("Fail to Reject H0: Non-Stationary (I(1))", "Reject H0: Stationary (I(0))")

section: 5 Step 4: Model Identification via ACF and PACF
text:
5 Step 4: Model Identification via ACF and PACF

5.1 Purpose
To identify candidate autoregressive orders \(p\) by inspecting the empirical autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation functions.


5.2 Statistical Concept
Under the Efficient Market Hypothesis, returns should behave as white noise with all autocorrelations \(\rho_k = 0\) for \(k \geq 1\). Under non-synchronous trading, a small but statistically significant spike occurs at lag 1 in the PACF (\(\phi_{11} > 0\)), while all higher-order partial autocorrelations vanish.
The 95% Bartlett confidence envelope for sample size \(n = 1,600\) is:
\[
\text{CI}_{0.95} = \pm \frac{1.96}{\sqrt{1600}} = \pm \frac{1.96}{40} = \pm 0.0490.
\]


5.3 R Implementation

6 Step 5: Model Estimation and Parameter Significance

6.1 Purpose
To estimate the parameters of the candidate models via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) and evaluate parameter significance and stationarity.


6.2 R Implementation


Code
# Fit candidate models
m0 <- stats::arima(train, order = c(0, 0, 0)) # White noise with drift
m1 <- stats::arima(train, order = c(1, 0, 0)) # AR(1)
m2 <- stats::arima(train, order = c(2, 0, 0)) # AR(2)
m3 <- stats::arima(train, order = c(3, 0, 0)) # AR(3)

# Function to extract coefficients and p-values
extract_ar_table <- function(m, p, name) {
  if (p == 0) {
    coefs <- m$coef["intercept"]
    ses   <- sqrt(m$var.coef["intercept", "intercept"])
  } else {
    coefs <- c(m$coef[1:p], m$coef["intercept"])
    ses   <- sqrt(diag(m$var.coef))[c(1:p, length(m$coef))]
  }
  t_val <- coefs / ses
  p_val <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(t_val)))
  
  data.frame(
    Model     = name,
    Parameter = names(coefs),
    Estimate  = round(coefs, 4),
    SE        = round(ses, 4),
    t_stat    = round(t_val, 3),
    p_value   = format.pval(p_val, eps = 0.001, digits = 3)
  )
}

param_summary <- rbind(
  extract_ar_table(m0, 0, "AR(0) / WN"),
  extract_ar_table(m1, 1, "AR(1)"),
  extract_ar_table(m2, 2, "AR(2)"),
  extract_ar_table(m3, 3, "AR(3)")
)

7.3 The Crucial Financial Insight: Statistical vs Economic Significance






ImportantWhy an \(\text{AR}(1)\) Model Cannot Beat the Market




Statistical Significance (\(p = 0.0066\)): The large sample size (\(n = 1,600\)) provides high statistical power, detecting small deviations from zero (\(R^2 = \phi_1^2 \approx 0.0678^2 \approx 0.46\%\)).
Economic Insignificance: The proportion of variance explained by the model is less than half of one percent (\(0.46\%\)). A \(1\%\) return yesterday predicts only a \(0.068\%\) return today.
Transaction Costs: Typical bid-ask spreads, broker commissions, and execution slippage in equity index futures during the 1990s were \(0.10\%\) to \(0.20\%\) per round-trip trade—far exceeding the \(0.068\%\) predicted move.
Hence, the \(\text{AR}(1)\) model is consistent with the Weak-Form Efficient Market Hypothesis after accounting for institutional transaction costs.

8 Step 7: Model Diagnostics & Assessment of Stylized Facts

8.1 Purpose
To test whether residuals satisfy white noise conditions and explore non-linear volatility clustering.


8.2 Statistical Concept

Linear Autocorrelation: Tested using the Ljung–Box Portmanteau test with adjusted degrees of freedom \(df = K - p\).
Normality & Fat Tails: Evaluated via Q–Q plot and Shapiro–Wilk test.
Non-Linear Dependence (ARCH Effect): Evaluated by testing for autocorrelation in squared residuals \(\hat{e}_t^2\). Even when \(\operatorname{Cov}(e_t, e_{t-k}) = 0\), if \(\operatorname{Cov}(e_t^2, e_{t-k}^2) \neq 0\), the process exhibits conditional heteroscedasticity.



8.3 R Implementation


Code
res_ar1 <- residuals(m1)
std_res <- res_ar1 / sqrt(m1$sigma2)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3.8, 4, 2.5, 1))

Modeling Takeaway: The linear \(\text{AR}(1)\) model adequately captures the conditional mean \(E[r_t \mid \mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\), but fails to model the conditional variance \(\operatorname{Var}(r_t \mid \mathcal{F}_{t-1})\). This empirical finding provides the motivation for GARCH(1,1) modeling.

9.1 Purpose
To compute 259-day-ahead dynamic forecasts over the holdout test horizon (mid-1997 to 1998) and evaluate accuracy against the Martingale benchmark.

Rapid Mean Reversion: Because \(\hat{\phi}_1 = 0.0678 \ll 1\), dynamic multi-step point forecasts revert to the unconditional mean \(\hat{\mu} = +0.047\%\) within two trading days.
Predictive Comparison: The \(\text{AR}(1)\) model achieves an out-of-sample \(\text{MAE} = 0.8104\) and \(\text{RMSE} = 1.0485\), which is virtually indistinguishable from the \(\text{AR}(0)\) Martingale Difference benchmark (\(\text{MAE} = 0.8102, \text{RMSE} = 1.0483\)).

section: 10 Step 9: Financial Engineering Discussion, Limitations & Defense Preparation
text:
10 Step 9: Financial Engineering Discussion, Limitations & Defense Preparation

10.1 Key Takeaways

Market Microstructure Autocorrelation: The FTSE 100 exhibits statistically significant positive first-order autocorrelation (\(\hat{\phi}_1 = 0.0678, p = 0.0066\)) due to non-synchronous trading of composite index constituents.
Economic vs Statistical Significance: An \(R^2\) of \(0.46\%\) cannot overcome execution costs, preserving the validity of the Weak-Form Efficient Market Hypothesis.
The Limits of Linear AR Models: While the \(\text{AR}(1)\) filters out all linear dependence in returns, its residuals violate the constant variance assumption. The presence of significant autocorrelation in squared residuals (\(\hat{e}_t^2\)) demonstrates the necessity of conditional heteroscedasticity models (ARCH/GARCH).



10.2 Anticipated Academic Defense Questions & Model Answers






ImportantQuestion 1: If markets are efficient, why did you find a statistically significant AR(1) coefficient?



Model Answer: In broad market capitalization indices such as the FTSE 100, index constituents do not trade at identical frequencies. As proven by Lo and MacKinlay (1990), non-synchronous trading causes information absorbed by liquid large-caps to appear with a one-day lag in less liquid small-caps, creating spurious positive index autocorrelation. However, the \(R^2\) is only \(0.46\%\), which is smaller than typical transaction costs (\(0.10\text{--}0.20\%\)). Therefore, the market is efficient in an economic sense.








ImportantQuestion 2: Why do linear residuals pass the Ljung–Box test while squared residuals fail?



Model Answer: The linear Ljung–Box test evaluates whether \(\operatorname{Cov}(e_t, e_{t-k}) = 0\). Because returns are linearly uncorrelated, the linear test passes (\(p = 0.308\)). However, independence requires \(\operatorname{Cov}(g(e_t), h(e_{t-k})) = 0\) for all functions \(g\) and \(h\). The squared residuals \(\hat{e}_t^2\) capture volatility magnitude. Because financial volatility clusters over time, \(\operatorname{Cov}(e_t^2, e_{t-k}^2) \neq 0\), causing the squared test to fail (\(p < 0.0001\)) and revealing the ARCH effect.








ImportantQuestion 3: Why does the AR(1) forecast flatline after just two days?



Model Answer: The speed of mean reversion in an \(\text{AR}(1)\) process is governed by the magnitude of \(|\phi_1|\). Since \(\hat{\phi}_1 = 0.0678\), the forecast at horizon \(h\) is \(\hat{r}_{n+h} = \mu + \phi_1^h (r_n - \mu)\). For \(h = 2\), \(\phi_1^2 = 0.0046 \approx 0\), meaning \(99.5\%\) of any initial return shock is dissipated within 48 trading hours, converging to the unconditional drift \(\mu\).

title: Chapter 1 · Introduction to Time Series
text:
A time series is a sequence of observations \(Y_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_n\) recorded sequentially through time. Unlike classical cross-sectional statistics where observations are assumed to be independent and identically distributed (\(i.i.d.\)), the defining feature of time series is temporal dependence: consecutive or nearby observations are frequently correlated with one another.


According to Cryer and Chan (Chapter 1), the objectives are twofold:

Descriptive & Mechanistic Understanding: To model and understand the underlying stochastic mechanism that generated the observed sequence.
Forecasting: To predict future values \(Y_{n+h}\) based on the series history \(\{Y_1, \dots, Y_n\}\) and other explanatory covariates.




Cryer & Chan emphasize the iterative three-stage modeling cycle proposed by Box and Jenkins (1976):
       ┌───────────────────────────────┐
       │   1. Model Specification      │ <─────────┐
       │   (Tentative Identification)  │           │
       └──────────────┬────────────────┘           │ (Revise if
                      │                            │  inadequate)
                      ▼                            │
       ┌───────────────────────────────┐           │
       │   2. Model Fitting            │           │
       │   (Parameter Estimation)      │           │
       └──────────────┬────────────────┘           │
                      │                            │
                      ▼                            │
       ┌───────────────────────────────┐           │
       │   3. Model Diagnostics        │ ──────────┘
       │   (Residual Checking & Tests) │
       └──────────────┬────────────────┘
                      │ (Adequate model)
                      ▼
       ┌───────────────────────────────┐
       │   Forecasting & Application   │
       └───────────────────────────────┘

Model Specification (Identification): Using visual time plots, sample autocorrelations, and domain knowledge to tentatively select candidate model classes (e.g., AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA).

Principle of Parsimony: The chosen model should contain the smallest number of parameters that adequately describes the data (“Everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler” — Albert Einstein).

Model Fitting (Estimation): Estimating unknown parameters using maximum likelihood or least squares.
Model Diagnostics: Examining model residuals to verify whether assumptions hold (e.g., checking that residuals resemble uncorrelated white noise).

3 Textbook Case Studies (Section 1.1)
Chapter 1 introduces five historical and industrial time series demonstrating distinct statistical properties:

3.1 Case 1: Annual Rainfall in Los Angeles (larain)
The larain dataset records annual precipitation (in inches) in Los Angeles over more than 100 years (1878–1992).


Code
data(larain)

plot(
  larain,
  ylab = "Inches",
  xlab = "Year",
  type = "o",
  pch = 16,
  col = primary_col,
  main = "Annual Rainfall in Los Angeles"
)
grid(col = grid_col)








Figure 1: Exhibit 1.1: Annual precipitation recorded in Los Angeles, California (1878–1992).





To examine whether consecutive years are statistically dependent, we construct the lag-1 scatterplot (\(Y_t\) versus \(Y_{t-1}\)) using zlag().


Code
plot(
  y = larain,
  x = zlag(larain),
  ylab = "Current Year Rainfall (inches)",
  xlab = "Previous Year Rainfall (inches)",
  pch = 19,
  col = point_col,
  main = "LA Rainfall vs. Previous Year"
)
grid(col = grid_col)
abline(h = mean(larain), v = mean(larain), lty = 2, col = "gray50")

# Compute lag-1 sample autocorrelation
r1_larain <- cor(larain[-1], zlag(larain)[-1])








Figure 2: Exhibit 1.2: Scatterplot of current year rainfall versus previous year rainfall.





Interpretation: The scatterplot displays a circular, unorganized cloud of points with an empirical lag-1 correlation of \(r_1 \approx -0.033\). Extremely wet years (such as 1883 with 40 inches) can be followed by average or dry years. Past rainfall provides virtually no linear predictive power for next year’s rainfall; this series behaves like independent white noise.



3.2 Case 2: Industrial Chemical Process (color)
The color dataset tracks color intensity across 35 consecutive batches in a chemical manufacturing process.


Code

plot(
  color,
  ylab = "Color Property",
  xlab = "Batch",
  type = "o",
  pch = 16,
  col = primary_col,
  main = "Chemical Process: Batch Color Property"
)

We now plot batch color \(Y_t\) against the previous batch \(Y_{t-1}\):

Interpretation: Unlike rainfall, neighboring batches show positive temporal persistence with a correlation of \(r_1 \approx 0.55\). Low values tend to follow low values, and high values follow high values, making first-order autoregressive modeling appropriate.

title: Empirical Modeling of Autoregressive Processes
text:
This empirical study provides an end-to-end, reproducible implementation of the Autoregressive (\(AR(p)\)) model within the classic Box–Jenkins framework. Using the historical annual Canadian Lynx trappings series (1821–1934, \(n = 114\)), we systematically execute data integrity validation, exploratory data analysis, stationarity testing, model identification via ACF/PACF, maximum likelihood parameter estimation, multi-criteria model selection, residual diagnostic checking, and out-of-sample dynamic forecasting with prediction intervals.
All computations are executed natively in R with zero fabricated metrics. The workflow illustrates how to defend modeling decisions with statistical rigor, explaining why parsimonious criteria (such as BIC) and out-of-sample predictive accuracy prevent in-sample overfitting.

title: Empirical Modeling of Autoregressive Processes
text:
1 Theoretical Framework of the \(AR(p)\) Model
An Autoregressive process of order \(p\), denoted \(\text{AR}(p)\), models the current observation \(Y_t\) as a linear combination of its \(p\) most recent past values plus an exogenous stochastic shock:
\[
Y_t = c + \phi_1 Y_{t-1} + \phi_2 Y_{t-2} + \dots + \phi_p Y_{t-p} + e_t,
\]
where:

\(c = \mu(1 - \sum_{i=1}^p \phi_i)\) is the constant term related to the unconditional process mean \(\mu = E(Y_t)\).
\(\phi_1, \phi_2, \dots, \phi_p\) are the autoregressive coefficients.
\(\{e_t\} \stackrel{i.i.d.}{\sim} \mathcal{W}\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_e^2)\) is a Gaussian white noise innovation sequence with \(E(e_t) = 0\), \(\operatorname{Var}(e_t) = \sigma_e^2\), and \(\operatorname{Cov}(e_t, e_s) = 0\) for \(t \neq s\).

Using the backshift (lag) operator \(B\), where \(B^k Y_t = Y_{t-k}\), the model is concisely expressed as:
\[
\Phi(B) Y_t = c + e_t, \qquad \text{where } \Phi(B) = 1 - \phi_1 B - \phi_2 B^2 - \dots - \phi_p B^p.
\]

1.1 Stationarity and Invertibility Conditions
An \(\text{AR}(p)\) process is weakly (covariance) stationary if and only if all roots of the characteristic equation
\[
\Phi(z) = 1 - \phi_1 z - \phi_2 z^2 - \dots - \phi_p z^p = 0
\]
lie strictly outside the complex unit circle, that is, \(|z_j| > 1\) for all \(j = 1, \dots, p\).
For an \(\text{AR}(1)\) process, this reduces to \(|\phi_1| < 1\). For an \(\text{AR}(2)\) process, the stationarity region forms a triangular parameter space:
\[
\phi_1 + \phi_2 < 1, \qquad \phi_2 - \phi_1 < 1, \qquad |\phi_2| < 1.
\]
When \(\phi_1^2 + 4\phi_2 < 0\), the roots of the characteristic equation form a complex conjugate pair \(z_{1,2} = r e^{\pm i \theta}\), generating damped quasi-cyclical fluctuations with characteristic frequency \(\theta\) and average cycle length:
\[
\theta = \arccos\left(\frac{\phi_1}{2\sqrt{-\phi_2}}\right), \qquad T = \frac{2\pi}{\theta}.
\]


1.2 Theoretical Signatures of ACF and PACF

Cuts off abruptly after lag \(p\) (\(\phi_{kk} = 0, \forall k > p\))

This fundamental duality makes the Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF) the primary diagnostic tool for identifying the order \(p\) of an autoregressive process.

2 Step 1: Data Preparation and Integrity Check

2.1 Purpose
To inspect the structural properties of the raw dataset, confirm the sampling interval, test for missing values and duplicates, and compute standard descriptive statistics.


2.2 Statistical Concept
A time series must possess a consistent sampling grid without irregular timestamp gaps or corrupted values before applying linear time-invariant filters. Extreme skewness and heavy tails frequently violate Gaussian innovation assumptions, requiring variance-stabilizing non-linear transformations (such as Box–Cox or logarithmic transformations).


2.3 R Implementation


Code
# 1. Load data
data(lynx)
raw_ts <- lynx

# 2. Structural metadata
n_total   <- length(raw_ts)
start_yr  <- start(raw_ts)[1]
end_yr    <- end(raw_ts)[1]
freq_val  <- frequency(raw_ts)
has_na    <- any(is.na(raw_ts))
has_dups  <- any(duplicated(time(raw_ts)))

# 3. Variance stabilization (log10 transformation)
# Following Campbell & Walker (1977) and Cryer & Chan (2008),
# log10 transformation stabilizes cyclical amplitude.
y <- log10(raw_ts)

# 4. Out-of-sample partitioning: 100 observations train, 14 observations test
train <- window(y, end = 1920)
test  <- window(y, start = 1921)

# 5. Descriptive statistics function
calc_descriptives <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  m <- mean(x)
  s <- sd(x)
  skew <- sum((x - m)^3) / (n * s^3)
  kurt <- sum((x - m)^4) / (n * s^4) - 3
  c(
    N        = n,
    Mean     = m,
    SD       = s,
    Median   = median(x),
    IQR      = IQR(x),
    Min      = min(x),
    Max      = max(x),
    Skewness = skew,
    Kurtosis = kurt
  )
}

desc_table <- rbind(
  `Raw Lynx`       = calc_descriptives(raw_ts),
  `Log10 Lynx`     = calc_descriptives(y),
  `Train (1821-1920)` = calc_descriptives(train),
  `Test (1921-1934)`  = calc_descriptives(test)

3 Step 2: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

3.1 Purpose
To visually examine the temporal properties of the series, detect potential structural breaks or deterministic trends, and verify variance homogeneity.


3.2 Statistical Concept
Stationarity in the wide sense requires both a constant unconditional mean and a constant unconditional variance. If the local variance expands as the series level rises, the process is heteroscedastic. A logarithmic transformation converts multiplicative variance dynamics into additive, homoscedastic fluctuations.


3.3 R Implementation


Code
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(3.5, 4, 2, 1), oma = c(0, 0, 1, 0))

# Raw series
plot(raw_ts, col = "gray30", lwd = 1.2,
     ylab = "Trappings", xlab = "", main = "Annual Canadian Lynx Trappings (1821–1934)")
grid(col = "gray85")

# Log10 series with train/test division
plot(y, col = "steelblue", lwd = 1.5,
     ylab = expression(log[10](Trappings)), xlab = "Year",
     main = expression("Variance-Stabilized Series: " * Y[t] == log[10](Lynx[t])))
abline(v = 1920.5, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
text(1910, 3.7, "Train (1821–1920)", col = "gray20", cex = 0.85)

Top panel: Raw annual lynx trappings exhibiting cycle-dependent amplitude. Bottom panel: Log10 transformed series displaying stabilized cyclical amplitude.






3.4 Output Interpretation

The raw series demonstrates sharp, asymmetric peaks followed by prolonged troughs, with peak amplitudes varying dramatically between 1,500 and nearly 7,000 trappings.
In contrast, the \(\log_{10}\) transformed series exhibits stable oscillation bounds between \(1.5\) and \(3.85\), with uniform cycle amplitudes across the entire 114-year period.
The series displays a prominent, recurring quasi-cyclical rhythm of approximately 9 to 10 years, reflecting the famous predator–prey ecological cycle between the Canadian lynx and the snowshoe hare.



3.5 Sample Academic Writing

“Visual inspection of the raw lynx trappings reveals strong cyclical behavior accompanied by heteroscedastic volatility: cycle peaks reach higher amplitudes during high-abundance phases. Following the logarithmic transformation, the oscillations exhibit stable amplitude bounds throughout the 1821–1934 window, with no evident long-term deterministic drift. The series fluctuates regularly around an empirical mean of approximately 2.90, displaying clear quasi-periodic cycles.”

title: Empirical Modeling of Autoregressive Processes
section: 4 Step 3: Stationarity Assessment and Differencing Decision
text:
4 Step 3: Stationarity Assessment and Differencing Decision

4.1 Purpose
To formally test whether the series possesses a unit root (stochastic trend) or is stationary around a constant mean.


4.2 Statistical Concept
The Augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) test evaluates the null hypothesis of a unit root (\(H_0: \gamma = 0\)) against the alternative of covariance stationarity (\(H_1: \gamma < 0\)) in the test regression:
\[
\Delta Y_t = c + \beta t + \gamma Y_{t-1} + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \psi_i \Delta Y_{t-i} + \varepsilon_t.
\]
If \(H_0\) is rejected (\(p < 0.05\)), the process is stationary in levels (\(I(0)\)). Differencing an already stationary process (\(\nabla Y_t = Y_t - Y_{t-1}\)) is known as overdifferencing; it injects an artificial non-invertible moving average unit root (\(\theta = 1\)) into the innovation structure, inflating parameter variances and distorting long-term forecasts.


4.3 R Implementation


Code
# ADF test on the training series
adf_result <- adf.test(train, alternative = "stationary")

adf_summary <- data.frame(
  Test = "Augmented Dickey-Fuller",
  Lag_Order = adf_result$parameter,
  Test_Statistic = round(adf_result$statistic, 4),
  P_Value = adf_result$p.value,
  Conclusion = ifelse(adf_result$p.value <= 0.05, 
                      "Reject H0: Stationary (I(0))", 
                      "Fail to Reject H0: Unit Root (I(1))")
)

Because \(p < 0.01\), we decisively reject the null hypothesis of a unit root at the \(1\%\) significance level.
Methodological Decision: The series is covariance-stationary in levels. Therefore, no differencing is required (\(d = 0\)). We proceed with stationary \(\text{AR}(p)\) specifications in levels.

The test statistic of -4.6713 falls well into the critical rejection region (\(p < 0.01\)), rejecting the null hypothesis of a unit root. Consequently, the logarithmic lynx series is confirmed to be stationary in levels (\(I(0)\)). Differencing was deliberately avoided to prevent overdifferencing and the introduction of an artificial moving-average unit root.”

section: 5 Step 4: Model Identification via ACF and PACF
text:
5 Step 4: Model Identification via ACF and PACF

5.1 Purpose
To analyze empirical autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation functions to determine candidate autoregressive orders (\(p\)).


5.2 Statistical Concept
For an \(\text{AR}(p)\) process: 1. Sample Autocorrelation Function (ACF): Satisfies the Yule–Walker difference equations, generating damped exponential decay or damped sinusoidal waves. 2. Sample Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF): Measures the correlation between \(Y_t\) and \(Y_{t-k}\) after filtering out the linear dependence explained by intermediate lags \(Y_{t-1}, \dots, Y_{t-k+1}\). Theoretical PACF cuts off sharply to zero for all lags \(k > p\):
\[
\phi_{kk} = 0 \quad \text{for all } k > p.
\]
Under the null hypothesis of an \(\text{AR}(p)\) process, sample PACF values beyond lag \(p\) are asymptotically normal with variance \(1/n\), yielding Bartlett 95% confidence intervals at:
\[
\text{CI}_{0.95} = \pm \frac{1.96}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]


5.3 R Implementation


Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))

# ACF
acf(train, lag.max = 15, main = "Sample Autocorrelation (ACF)",
    col = "gray20", lwd = 2, ylim = c(-0.8, 1))
grid(col = "gray90")

# PACF
pacf(train, lag.max = 15, main = "Sample Partial Autocorrelation (PACF)",
     col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, ylim = c(-0.8, 1))
grid(col = "gray90")

The sample partial autocorrelation function displays large, statistically significant coefficients at lag 1 (\(\hat{\phi}_{11} = 0.780\)) and lag 2 (\(\hat{\phi}_{22} = -0.711\)), followed by an immediate drop within the 95% Bartlett bounds (\(\pm 1.96/\sqrt{100} = \pm 0.196\)). This distinct cutoff pattern provides strong empirical evidence in favor of an \(\text{AR}(2)\) specification, while \(\text{AR}(1)\), \(\text{AR}(3)\), and \(\text{AR}(4)\) are retained as competitive candidates.”

6 Step 5: Model Estimation and Parameter Significance

6.1 Purpose
To estimate the parameters of the candidate models using Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), extract standard errors, test coefficient significance, and evaluate characteristic roots.


6.2 Statistical Concept
Parameters are estimated via Maximum Likelihood Estimation initialized through the Kalman filter. The asymptotic covariance matrix of the estimators \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\) is obtained from the inverse Fisher Information matrix:
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}) = \mathcal{I}^{-1}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}).
\]
For each coefficient, we evaluate the Wald statistic:
\[
t = \frac{\hat{\phi}_j}{\operatorname{SE}(\hat{\phi}_j)} \stackrel{a}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, 1).
\]
Coefficients are statistically significant at \(\alpha = 0.05\) if \(|t| > 1.96\) (\(p < 0.05\)).


6.3 R Implementation


Code
# Fit candidate models via stats::arima (MLE)
m1 <- stats::arima(train, order = c(1, 0, 0))
m2 <- stats::arima(train, order = c(2, 0, 0))
m3 <- stats::arima(train, order = c(3, 0, 0))
m4 <- stats::arima(train, order = c(4, 0, 0))

# Extraction helper function
extract_ar_table <- function(m, p, model_name) {
  coefs <- m$coef[1:p]
  ses   <- sqrt(diag(m$var.coef))[1:p]
  t_val <- coefs / ses
  p_val <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(t_val)))
  
  data.frame(
    Model     = model_name,
    Parameter = names(coefs),
    Estimate  = round(coefs, 4),
    SE        = round(ses, 4),
    t_stat    = round(t_val, 3),
    p_value   = format.pval(p_val, eps = 0.001, digits = 3)
  )
}

param_summary <- rbind(
  extract_ar_table(m1, 1, "AR(1)"),
  extract_ar_table(m2, 2, "AR(2)"),
  extract_ar_table(m3, 3, "AR(3)"),

7 Step 6: Multi-Criteria Model Selection

7.1 Purpose
To compare candidate models across goodness-of-fit, parameter penalty criteria, and residual variance, explaining why model choice cannot rely on AIC alone.


7.2 Statistical Concept
Goodness-of-fit naturally improves as additional lags are appended to an autoregressive model. Penalized likelihood criteria balance in-sample fit against model complexity:
\[
\text{AIC} = -2\ln(\hat{L}) + 2k,
\]
\[
\text{BIC} = -2\ln(\hat{L}) + k\ln(n),
\]
where \(k\) is the total number of estimated parameters (including autoregressive parameters, constant, and innovation variance \(\sigma_e^2\)), and \(n\) is the training sample size (\(n = 100\)).


7.3 Why Model Selection Cannot Rely on AIC Alone






NoteCritical Distinction Between AIC and BIC




AIC is asymptotically efficient; its penalty (\(2k\)) reflects the Kullback–Leibler information discrepancy. However, in small-to-moderate samples, AIC has a non-zero probability of over-parameterizing autoregressive processes because the penalty does not grow with sample size.
BIC is dimensionally consistent; because \(\ln(n) = \ln(100) \approx 4.605 > 2\), BIC penalizes additional coefficients more than twice as heavily as AIC. Under the true finite \(\text{AR}(p)\) model, the probability that BIC selects the correct order approaches 1 as \(n \to \infty\).
Relying on AIC alone risks selecting overfitted specifications that capture in-sample noise at the expense of out-of-sample forecast accuracy.





7.4 R Implementation


Code
calc_bic <- function(m, n_obs) {
  k <- length(m$coef) + 1 # AR terms + intercept + sigma^2
  -2 * m$loglik + k * log(n_obs)
}

8 Step 7: Model Diagnostics and Residual Verification

8.1 Purpose
To rigorously check that the residuals of the fitted \(\text{AR}(2)\) model satisfy white noise assumptions: zero mean, homoscedasticity, absence of serial correlation, and approximate Gaussianity.


8.2 Statistical Concept
Let \(\hat{e}_t = Y_t - \hat{Y}_t\) be the model residuals. 1. Ljung–Box Portmanteau Test: Evaluates whether residual autocorrelations up to lag \(K\) are jointly zero: \[
   Q^*(K) = n(n + 2) \sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{\hat{r}_k^2(\hat{e})}{n - k} \stackrel{H_0}{\sim} \chi^2(K - p),
   \] where degrees of freedom must be adjusted by subtracting the \(p = 2\) estimated AR coefficients (\(df = K - p\)). 2. Normality: Assessed via the Shapiro–Wilk test and Normal Quantile–Quantile (Q–Q) plots.


8.3 R Implementation


Code

std_res <- res_ar2 / sqrt(m2$sigma2)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3.8, 4, 2.5, 1))

abline(h = c(-2, 2), col = "firebrick", lty = 2)

9 Step 8: Out-of-Sample Forecasting and Empirical Evaluation

9.1 Purpose
To generate multi-step dynamic out-of-sample forecasts over the 14-year post-sample horizon (1921–1934), compute prediction intervals, and evaluate forecast accuracy against the competing specifications.


9.2 Statistical Concept
For an \(\text{AR}(2)\) process, point forecasts \(\hat{Y}_{n+h|n}\) are computed recursively:
\[
\hat{Y}_{n+1|n} = c + \phi_1 Y_n + \phi_2 Y_{n-1},
\]
\[
\hat{Y}_{n+h|n} = c + \phi_1 \hat{Y}_{n+h-1|n} + \phi_2 \hat{Y}_{n+h-2|n} \quad (h \geq 2).
\]
The \(100(1 - \alpha)\%\) prediction interval at horizon \(h\) is given by:
\[
\hat{Y}_{n+h|n} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \sigma_e \sqrt{\sum_{j=0}^{h-1} \psi_j^2},
\]
where \(\psi_j\) are the impulse-response coefficients from the Wold representation \(Y_t = \mu + \sum_{j=0}^\infty \psi_j e_{t-j}\).
Out-of-sample performance is quantified on the reserved test partition (\(h = 14\)) using:

Mean Absolute Error (MAE): \(\frac{1}{h}\sum_{i=1}^h |Y_{n+i} - \hat{Y}_{n+i|n}|\)
Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): \(\sqrt{\frac{1}{h}\sum_{i=1}^h (Y_{n+i} - \hat{Y}_{n+i|n})^2}\)
Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE): \(\frac{100\%}{h}\sum_{i=1}^h \left|\frac{Y_{n+i} - \hat{Y}_{n+i|n}}{Y_{n+i}}\right|\)



9.3 R Implementation


Code
# Generate 14-step-ahead forecasts for all models

pi_95_lower <- pred_val - 1.960 * se_val
pi_95_upper <- pred_val + 1.960 * se_val

  mae  <- mean(abs(actual - predicted))
  rmse <- sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))
  mape <- mean(abs((actual - predicted) / actual)) * 100
  c(MAE = mae, RMSE = rmse, MAPE = mape)
}

section: 10 Step 9: Academic Discussion, Limitations, and Defense Preparation
text:
10 Step 9: Academic Discussion, Limitations, and Defense Preparation

10.1 Comprehensive Summary of Findings

Identification: The sample PACF exhibited a distinct two-lag cutoff (\(\hat{\phi}_{11} = 0.780, \hat{\phi}_{22} = -0.711\)), while the ACF showed damped sinusoidal oscillation with a 9.69-year cycle.
Estimation & Stationarity: The \(\text{AR}(2)\) parameter estimates (\(\hat{\phi}_1 = 1.3693, \hat{\phi}_2 = -0.7385\)) possess complex roots with modulus \(1.1637 > 1\), confirming covariance stationarity.
Model Selection: BIC (\(16.16\)) and parameter significance strictly favored \(\text{AR}(2)\) over \(\text{AR}(3)\) and \(\text{AR}(4)\), avoiding the overfitting tendency of AIC.
Validation: Residuals satisfied all white noise criteria (\(p > 0.10\) for Ljung–Box tests) and conformed to normality (\(W = 0.991, p = 0.746\)).
Forecasting: Out-of-sample validation confirmed \(\text{AR}(2)\) as the most accurate predictive specification (\(\text{RMSE} = 0.2824\)).



10.2 Methodological Limitations

Linearity vs Non-linear Dynamics: The linear \(\text{AR}(2)\) model assumes symmetric cycles. In predator–prey ecology, population declines are often steeper than the growth phase. Advanced literature (Tong, 1990) models this asymmetry using Self-Exciting Threshold Autoregressive (SETAR) models.
Asymptotic Normality: Prediction intervals rely on Gaussian white noise innovations. While the logarithmic transformation normalized residuals, real-world extreme shocks can induce fat-tailed distributions requiring bootstrap prediction intervals.



10.3 Anticipated Academic Defense Questions & Model Answers






ImportantQuestion 1: Why did you not difference the series before fitting an AR model?



Model Answer: The Augmented Dickey–Fuller test on the training partition yielded \(\text{DF} = -4.6713\) with \(p < 0.01\), firmly rejecting the null hypothesis of a unit root. Differencing a series that is already stationary (\(I(0)\)) constitutes overdifferencing. Overdifferencing introduces an artificial moving average unit root (\(\theta = 1\)), increases residual variance, and degrades long-term forecasts.








ImportantQuestion 2: AR(4) achieved a lower AIC than AR(2). Why did you select AR(2)?



Model Answer: AIC penalizes complexity by \(2k\), which has a well-known asymptotic probability of selecting over-parameterized models in finite samples. BIC uses \(k\ln(n) \approx 4.605k\), which penalizes redundant parameters more severely and is consistent. In our data, the 3rd and 4th lag coefficients were statistically insignificant (\(p > 0.05\)). Furthermore, out-of-sample evaluation demonstrated that \(\text{AR}(2)\) achieved lower MAE and RMSE than \(\text{AR}(4)\), confirming that the lower AIC of \(\text{AR}(4)\) was the result of in-sample overfitting.








ImportantQuestion 3: How do you justify the degrees of freedom used in the Ljung–Box test?



Model Answer: When testing the residuals of an estimated \(\text{AR}(p)\) model, the test statistic does not follow a \(\chi^2(K)\) distribution because the residuals are estimated from the data, which consumes degrees of freedom. Box and Pierce (1970) and Ljung and Box (1978) established that the null distribution is asymptotically \(\chi^2(K - p)\). Failing to subtract the \(p = 2\) estimated parameters would lead to overly conservative test statistics and inflated \(p\)-values.

title: Gold Price Forecasting Using Five Classical Time-Series Models
text:
Gold (XAU) occupies a singular role in quantitative finance, serving simultaneously as a global monetary reserve asset, a systemic risk hedge, an inflation counter-weight, and an actively traded industrial and jewelry commodity. Developing disciplined econometric forecasts of gold price dynamics is a critical priority for central banks, sovereign wealth institutions, bullion dealers, and financial engineers.
This study implements an academically rigorous and fully reproducible empirical investigation of gold price forecasting across five classical time-series specifications:

Autoregressive Model — \(\text{AR}(p)\)
Moving Average Model — \(\text{MA}(q)\)
Autoregressive Moving Average Model — \(\text{ARMA}(p, q)\)
Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average — \(\text{SARIMA}(p, d, q)(P, D, Q)[s]\)
Simple Exponential Smoothing — \(\text{SES}\)

Using \(2,971\) daily market observations from Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME Group) COMEX Continuous Gold Futures (GC=F) spanning January 2015 to October 2026, we implement a strict chronological \(80\%/20\%\) in-sample estimation and out-of-sample holdout protocol.
Key empirical findings:

Non-Stationarity in Levels (\(I(1)\)): The Augmented Dickey–Fuller test on price levels yields \(\text{ADF} = -1.4591\) (\(p = 0.8073\)), failing to reject the presence of a unit root. First-differencing yields strong stationarity (\(\text{ADF} = -14.878, p < 0.01\)), confirming that the series requires integration order \(d=1\).
Holdout Predictive Superiority: On the unobserved 595-day out-of-sample test horizon (June 2024 to October 2026), \(\text{ARIMA}(0,1,0)\) with drift achieved the highest forecasting accuracy (\(\text{MAE} = \$1,164.18\), \(\text{RMSE} = \$1,390.75\), \(\text{MAPE} = 28.80\%\)). By estimating a positive drift term (\(\hat{c} \approx \$0.48\)/day), it captured the persistent secular rally in bullion prices driven by geopolitical stress and central bank de-dollarization.
Martingale Benchmark Validation: Classical zero-drift models (\(\text{SES}\), \(\text{AR}(1)\), \(\text{MA}(1)\), \(\text{ARMA}(1,1)\)) produced flat multi-step forecast trajectories (\(\text{RMSE} \approx \$1,548.94\), \(\text{MAPE} \approx 32.39\%\)), directly reflecting the Martingale Difference Hypothesis where the conditional expectation of future asset prices is dominated by the most recent price observation.

text:
1 1. Introduction and Research Objectives

1.1 Background and Motivation
Gold holds a unique status in modern asset pricing: - As a physical commodity, its supply is constrained by mining extraction costs and scrap recycling, while physical demand is driven by jewelry and advanced electronics manufacturing. - As a monetary store of value, its price is fundamentally determined by macroeconomic drivers: real interest rates (U.S. TIPS yields), currency valuations (the U.S. Dollar Index, DXY), sovereign reserve accumulation, and global geopolitical tail risk.
Because market participants, treasury departments, and risk managers require objective, model-based price trajectory benchmarks, constructing and comparing time-series models within the classic Box–Jenkins framework is an indispensable analytical foundation.


1.2 Research Objectives
The specific empirical objectives are: 1. Conduct an exhaustive exploratory data analysis of historical gold prices, examining secular trends, empirical distributions (levels vs. log returns), annual volatility regimes, and descriptive statistics across the last five years. 2. Formally test for stationarity and determine the integration order \(d\) through graphical rolling statistics, autocorrelation analysis, and the Augmented Dickey–Fuller (\(\text{ADF}\)) unit root test. 3. Formulate, estimate, and select optimal candidate specifications for each of the five target model families using Information Criteria (\(\text{AIC}\), \(\text{BIC}\)) and residual diagnostics. 4. Execute uniform out-of-sample forecasts over an unobserved \(20\%\) chronological holdout sample under identical forecast horizons and origins. 5. Provide multi-metric evaluation (\(\text{MAE}\), \(\text{RMSE}\), \(\text{MAPE}\)), generate both publication-grade static figures and interactive ggplot2/plotly visualization suites, and synthesize financial and econometric conclusions.

title: Gold Price Forecasting Using Five Classical Time-Series Models
text:
2 2. Gold Price Dataset and Source

2.1 Data Provenance and Variable Specification
To ensure absolute academic integrity and full reproducibility, all empirical findings are derived from the official market series without synthetic fabrication:

Source: Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME Group) COMEX Continuous Active Gold Futures (GC=F), retrieved via Yahoo Finance.
Underlying: Physical Gold (XAU), standard delivery.
Target Variable: Gold Closing Settlement Price Level (price).
Unit & Currency: USD per troy ounce ($/oz).
Observation Frequency: Daily (active trading business days, Monday through Friday, excluding exchange holidays).
Sample Window: 2 January 2015 to 26 October 2026 (\(N = 2,971\) active trading day records).
Raw File Paths:

Standard level series: data/gold_price.csv
Full OHLCV daily market dataset: data/gold_price_daily.csv
Monthly aggregate dataset: data/gold_price_monthly.csv

Acquisition Script: Fully documented and reproducible script in scripts/download_gold_data.R.



2.2 Price Level vs. Return Differencing
In financial time series, analysts frequently distinguish between forecasting: 1. The Price Level (\(P_t\)): Non-stationary, persistent, and directly relevant for balance sheet valuation, budgeting, and long-term procurement. 2. Log Returns (\(r_t = 100 \times \ln(P_t / P_{t-1})\)) or First Differences (\(\Delta P_t = P_t - P_{t-1}\)): Stationary (\(I(0)\)), eliminating stochastic trend persistence.
As mandated by our objective, the primary forecasting target is the gold price level. When stationary models (\(\text{AR}\), \(\text{MA}\), \(\text{ARMA}\)) require differenced series for estimation, forecasts are integrated back to price levels to guarantee fair, out-of-sample comparability against integrated models (\(\text{ARIMA/SARIMA}\)) and \(\text{SES}\).

5 5. Stationarity Analysis

5.1 Theoretical Foundation
A stochastic time series \(\{Y_t\}\) is defined as weakly (covariance) stationary if and only if: 1. Constant Mean: \(E[Y_t] = \mu\) for all \(t\). 2. Constant Finite Variance: \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_t) = \sigma^2 < \infty\) for all \(t\). 3. Time-Invariant Autocovariance: \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t-k}) = \gamma_k\) depends exclusively on the displacement lag \(k\), and not on the absolute time index \(t\).
Financial asset price levels generally violate conditions (1) and (2) due to secular growth, inflation drift, and stochastic random walk trends (\(I(1)\) processes). Directly estimating autoregressive or moving average models on non-stationary levels produces spurious autocorrelations and invalid \(t\)-statistics.


5.2 Visual Diagnostics: Stationarity vs. Non-Stationarity
To visually illustrate the transition from non-stationarity to stationarity, we compare the gold price level alongside its 60-day rolling mean against the first-differenced series (\(\Delta P_t = P_t - P_{t-1}\)).

5.3 Formal Augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) Unit Root Test
The ADF test investigates the presence of a unit root using the regression: \[\Delta Y_t = \alpha + \beta t + \gamma Y_{t-1} + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \delta_i \Delta Y_{t-i} + e_t\]

Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)): \(\gamma = 0\) (the series contains a unit root, i.e., is non-stationary).
Alternative Hypothesis (\(H_1\)): \(\gamma < 0\) (the series is stationary).
Significance Threshold: \(\alpha = 0.05\).

  `p-value`            = c(sprintf("%.4f", adf_level$p.value), "< 0.01"),
  `Decision (α = 0.05)` = c("Fail to Reject H0 (Non-Stationary)", "Reject H0 (Stationary)"),

10 10. Out-of-Sample Forecast Generation and Evaluation

10.1 Generation of Point Forecasts
Each of the five models generates out-of-sample projections over the common holdout horizon \(h = 595\) days (\(2024\text{–}06\text{–}20\) to \(2026\text{–}10\text{–}26\)).

fc_ma     <- forecast(fit_ma1, h = h_test)
fc_arma   <- forecast(fit_arma11, h = h_test)
fc_sarima <- forecast(fit_sarima, h = h_test)
fc_ses    <- forecast(fit_ses, h = h_test)




10.2 Accuracy Metrics Formulation
We evaluate predictive performance on actual gold price levels using three standard metrics:

Mean Absolute Error (MAE): \[ \text{MAE} = \frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}}\sum_{t=1}^{n_{\text{test}}} |Y_t - \hat{Y}_t| \]
Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): \[ \text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}}\sum_{t=1}^{n_{\text{test}}} (Y_t - \hat{Y}_t)^2} \]
Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE): \[ \text{MAPE} = \frac{100\%}{n_{\text{test}}}\sum_{t=1}^{n_{\text{test}}} \left|\frac{Y_t - \hat{Y}_t}{Y_t}\right| \]



Code
y_test <- test_data$price

calc_accuracy <- function(actual, predicted) {
  err <- actual - predicted
  mae  <- mean(abs(err))
  rmse <- sqrt(mean(err^2))
  mape <- mean(abs(err / actual)) * 100
  c(MAE = mae, RMSE = rmse, MAPE = mape)
}

metrics_matrix <- rbind(
  `AR(1) integrated`     = calc_accuracy(y_test, as.numeric(fc_ar$mean)),
  `MA(1) integrated`     = calc_accuracy(y_test, as.numeric(fc_ma$mean)),
  `ARMA(1,1) integrated` = calc_accuracy(y_test, as.numeric(fc_arma$mean)),
  `SARIMA (Auto ARIMA)`  = calc_accuracy(y_test, as.numeric(fc_sarima$mean)),
  `Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES)` = calc_accuracy(y_test, as.numeric(fc_ses$mean))
)

13 13. Discussion and Financial Interpretation

13.1 1. Superiority of the Drift Specification
The automated SARIMA selection chose \(\text{ARIMA}(0, 1, 0)\) with a positive drift term (\(\hat{c} \approx \$0.48\)/day). This specification outperformed all zero-drift competitors by \(\$141.11\)/oz in MAE and \(\$158.19\)/oz in RMSE. Because physical gold experienced a sustained secular bull market driven by global central bank reserve purchases and structural inflation, incorporating the historical drift allowed the model to project an upward path rather than a static horizontal line.


13.2 2. Martingale Behavior in Zero-Drift Models
The zero-drift models (\(\text{SES}\), \(\text{AR}(1)\), \(\text{MA}(1)\), \(\text{ARMA}(1,1)\)) produced nearly identical flat forecast trajectories (\(\text{RMSE} \approx \$1,548.94\)). This behavior is consistent with the Martingale Difference Hypothesis (MDH) in financial asset pricing: \[ E[P_{t+h} \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = P_t \] In the absence of a drift parameter, any transient \(\text{AR}\) or \(\text{MA}\) shock decays rapidly within a few steps, causing long-horizon point forecasts to collapse to the last observed price level.


13.3 3. Role of Simple Exponential Smoothing as a Benchmark
\(\text{SES}\) estimated an optimal smoothing parameter of \(\alpha \approx 0.999\), indicating that the model places virtually all weight on the most recent observation. While mathematically parsimonious, SES serves as an essential baseline: any complex multi-parameter econometric model that fails to outperform SES imposes unwarranted parameter uncertainty without predictive reward.

text:
14 14. Limitations

Univariate Information Constraint: Univariate time-series models rely exclusively on past price history, ignoring exogenous macroeconomic drivers:

Real interest rates (U.S. 10-year TIPS yield).
Foreign exchange dynamics (U.S. Dollar Index, DXY).
Global geopolitical risk indices and central bank net purchases.

Conditional Homoskedasticity: Classical Box–Jenkins models assume constant disturbance variance \(\sigma^2\). As shown in the return distribution analysis, gold displays substantial volatility clustering, motivating hybrid \(\text{ARIMA-GARCH}\) specifications.
Multi-Step Uncertainty: Point forecasts over extended horizons (595 days) exhibit rapidly widening prediction intervals, reflecting the fundamental reality of market efficiency over multi-year horizons.

title: Gold Price Forecasting Using Five Classical Time-Series Models
text:
15 15. Conclusion
This study executed a comprehensive, reproducible empirical comparison of five classical time-series models for gold price forecasting using 2,971 daily CME COMEX gold futures records (2015–2026).

Unit Root Evidence: Gold price levels are non-stationary (\(I(1)\)), necessitating first-order differencing.
Top Out-of-Sample Model: \(\text{ARIMA}(0,1,0)\) with drift won the evaluation (\(\text{RMSE} = \$1,390.75\), \(\text{MAE} = \$1,164.18\), \(\text{MAPE} = 28.80\%\)).
Practical Takeaway: While statistical time-series models provide disciplined baselines for financial engineers, real-world hedging and portfolio management require combining univariate drift models with macroeconomic risk drivers and dynamic volatility modeling.

title: TD/TP 02 — Fundamental Mathematical Concepts
text:
1 Notation and Assumptions
Throughout this document, \(\{e_t\}\) denotes a zero-mean white noise process satisfying
\[
E(e_t) = 0, \qquad
\operatorname{Var}(e_t) = \sigma_e^2, \qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(e_t, e_s) = 0 \quad (t \neq s).
\]
A process \(\{Y_t\}\) is covariance stationary if

\(E(Y_t) = \mu\) for all \(t\) (constant mean), and
\(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t-k}) = \gamma_k\) for all \(t\) (autocovariance depends only on lag \(k\)).

The autocorrelation function (ACF) is defined as \[
\rho_k = \frac{\gamma_k}{\gamma_0}, \qquad k = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots
\]

title: TD/TP 02 — Fundamental Mathematical Concepts
text:
2 Exercise 2.4 — MA(1) Process
Given. Let \(\{e_t\}\) be zero-mean white noise and define \[
Y_t = e_t + \theta e_{t-1}, \qquad \theta \in \bigl\{3,\; \tfrac{1}{3}\bigr\}.
\]

2.1 Part (a): Autocorrelation function
Mean. \[
E(Y_t) = E(e_t) + \theta\, E(e_{t-1}) = 0.
\]
Variance. \[
\gamma_0 = \operatorname{Var}(Y_t)
         = \operatorname{Var}(e_t) + \theta^2 \operatorname{Var}(e_{t-1})
         = \sigma_e^2(1 + \theta^2).
\]
Lag-1 autocovariance. \[
\gamma_1 = \operatorname{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t-1})
         = E\bigl[(e_t + \theta e_{t-1})(e_{t-1} + \theta e_{t-2})\bigr]
         = \theta\, E(e_{t-1}^2)
         = \theta\sigma_e^2.
\]
Lag \(|k| \geq 2\). The sets \(\{t, t-1\}\) and \(\{t-k, t-k-1\}\) are disjoint, so \(\gamma_k = 0\).
ACF. \[
\rho_k = \begin{cases}
  1 & k = 0, \\[4pt]
  \dfrac{\theta}{1 + \theta^2} & |k| = 1, \\[6pt]
  0 & |k| \geq 2.
\end{cases}
\]
Evaluating at the two specified values:



\(\theta\)
\(\rho_1 = \theta/(1+\theta^2)\)




\(3\)
\(3/10 = 0.3\)


\(1/3\)
\((1/3)/(1 + 1/9) = (1/3)/(10/9) = 3/10 = 0.3\)



Both processes share identical ACFs.


2.2 Part (b): Identification from the sample ACF
Because \(\theta = 3\) and \(\theta = 1/3\) yield the same ACF, no estimator \(\hat{\rho}_k\) — however precise — can distinguish between them. This is a consequence of MA(1) invertibility aliasing: for any solution \(\theta\), the reciprocal \(1/\theta\) produces an equivalent ACF. Uniqueness is restored by imposing the invertibility condition \(|\theta| < 1\), which selects \(\theta = 1/3\).


Code
library(ggplot2)

sim_ma1 <- function(theta, n = 500) {
  e <- rnorm(n + 1)
  tail(e[-1] + theta * e[-(n + 1)], n)
}

y3   <- sim_ma1(3)
y1_3 <- sim_ma1(1 / 3)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
acf(y3,   main = expression(theta == 3),   lag.max = 10, ylim = c(-0.5, 1))
acf(y1_3, main = expression(theta == 1/3), lag.max = 10, ylim = c(-0.5, 1))





Sample ACFs for MA(1) with θ = 3 and θ = 1/3 (n = 500)

section: 3 Exercise 2.5 — Linear Trend Plus Stationary Component
text:
3 Exercise 2.5 — Linear Trend Plus Stationary Component
Given. \(Y_t = 5 + 2t + X_t\), where \(\{X_t\}\) is zero-mean stationary with autocovariance \(\gamma_k^X\).

3.1 Part (a): Mean function
\[
\mu_t = E(Y_t) = 5 + 2t + E(X_t) = 5 + 2t.
\]
The mean is a linear function of \(t\).


3.2 Part (b): Autocovariance function
Constants are absorbed by the expectation operator, so \[
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t-k})
  = \operatorname{Cov}(X_t, X_{t-k})
  = \gamma_k^X.
\]
The autocovariance depends only on the lag \(k\).


3.3 Part (c): Stationarity
\(\{Y_t\}\) is not stationary. Although the autocovariance satisfies the second condition, the mean \(\mu_t = 5 + 2t\) varies with \(t\), violating the first condition. Both conditions must hold simultaneously.

title: TD/TP 02 — Fundamental Mathematical Concepts
text:
4 Exercise 2.8 — Finite Linear Filter
Given. \(\{Y_t\}\) is stationary with mean \(\mu\) and autocovariance \(\gamma_k\). Define the linear filter \[
W_t = \sum_{j=1}^{n} c_j\, Y_{t-j+1},
\] for fixed constants \(c_1, \ldots, c_n\).
Claim. \(\{W_t\}\) is covariance stationary.
Proof.
Mean. \[
E(W_t) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} c_j\, E(Y_{t-j+1}) = \mu \sum_{j=1}^{n} c_j,
\] which is constant.
Autocovariance. By bilinearity of covariance, \[
\operatorname{Cov}(W_t, W_{t-k})
  = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} c_i c_j\,
    \operatorname{Cov}(Y_{t-i+1},\, Y_{t-k-j+1}).
\]
Since \(\{Y_t\}\) is stationary, \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{t-i+1}, Y_{t-k-j+1}) = \gamma_{k+j-i}\), which depends only on the lag. Therefore \[
\operatorname{Cov}(W_t, W_{t-k})
  = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} c_i c_j\, \gamma_{k+j-i},
\] a function of \(k\) alone. Hence \(\{W_t\}\) is covariance stationary. \(\blacksquare\)

title: TD/TP 02 — Fundamental Mathematical Concepts
text:
5 Exercise 2.9 — Differencing a Polynomial Trend
Given. \(Y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + X_t\), where \(\{X_t\}\) is zero-mean stationary with autocovariance \(\gamma_k^X\).

5.1 Part (a): First difference \(W_t = \nabla Y_t\)
\(\{Y_t\}\) is not stationary because \(E(Y_t) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t\) depends on \(t\).
Apply the first-difference operator \(\nabla\): \[
W_t = Y_t - Y_{t-1}
    = \bigl(\beta_0 + \beta_1 t + X_t\bigr) - \bigl(\beta_0 + \beta_1(t-1) + X_{t-1}\bigr)
    = \beta_1 + (X_t - X_{t-1}).
\]
Mean. \(E(W_t) = \beta_1\) (constant).
Autocovariance. \[
\operatorname{Cov}(W_t, W_{t-k})
  = \operatorname{Cov}(X_t - X_{t-1},\; X_{t-k} - X_{t-k-1})
  = 2\gamma_k^X - \gamma_{k-1}^X - \gamma_{k+1}^X,
\] which depends only on \(k\). Hence \(\{W_t\}\) is stationary. \(\blacksquare\)


5.2 Part (b): General polynomial trend of degree \(d\)
Let \(\mu_t\) be a polynomial in \(t\) of degree \(d\). The operator \(\nabla\) reduces the degree by one: \(\nabla \mu_t\) has degree \(d - 1\). By induction, \(\nabla^m \mu_t = 0\) for \(m \geq d\) (or equals a nonzero constant when \(m = d\)).

If \(m \geq d\): the polynomial part vanishes after \(m\) differences and \(\nabla^m X_t\) remains stationary (by Exercise 2.8), so \(\nabla^m Y_t\) is stationary.
If \(0 \leq m < d\): \(\nabla^m \mu_t\) is still a nonconstant polynomial in \(t\), so \(E(\nabla^m Y_t)\) depends on \(t\) and \(\nabla^m Y_t\) is not stationary.
